title: Adelheid Erica Amanda Mueller Nickel
summary: This brief biography was read during Adelheid’s memorial service at Calvary Lutheran Church in Stayton, Oregon.

title: The Call to St. Lucas Evangelical Lutheran Church
summary: In early October 1930, Adelheid Mueller received a formal call from St. Lucas Evangelical Lutheran Church, a Wisconsin-Synod congregation in Milwaukee. It was dated September 12, postmarked September 28. She was 23 at the time and had been teaching school in La Crosse, Wisconsin — her first job after graduating from Dr. Martin Luther College (Class of 1929). Adelheid evidently had learned that the call was coming and discussed it with her parents. Pastor Köhler’s letter mentions that Viola Oetchen, already a teacher at St. Lucas, was eager to have Adelheid as a roommate. For whatever reason, Adelheid made other living arrangements, renting a room from Albert and Margaret Nickel, two members of the church. The Nickels had a son named Hilbert, who sang in the St. Lucas choir ...

summary: The Frau Erica archive knows of five forebears who bore Anson as their first or middle name.. There may well be more, considering the size of families a couple generations in the past. Here are the five. If you know of others, please [contact the archivist](/contact).

title: Elizabeth Ann Mueller
summary: This obituary was published June 3, 2021, in the *Chicago Tribune*.

title: Carl de Haas and *Winke für Auswanderer*
summary: Carl de Haas, great- and great-great-grandfather to the McMillans of White Bear Lake, arrived on the Wisconsin frontier in 1847. *Winke für Auswanderer,* his booklet of advice for people considering emigration, was widely available in Germany and went through at least two printings and an expanded second edition.

title: *Winke für Auswanderer:* Hints for Emigrants
summary: Carl, his brother Richard, and nephew Eduard began their trip to New York by river steamer from Düsseldorf to Rotterdam, and by sea from Rotterdam to Havre and Cherbourg. It was an early introduction to seasickness, poor service, inedible food, overcharging, and too much baggage. Still, he encouraged others to make the trip.

title: II. In Havre and Cherbourg
summary: Their ship would not leave from Havre as promised, but from Cherbourg — and nearly a month late. They boarded the Union after three weeks in Cherbourg and were appalled at dreadful accommodations far below what they had been promised. Carl, who spoke some French, led a delegation ashore to confront the agents Herout & de Handel with their complaints. It was evening, time was short, they did what they could but did not succeed.

title: III. Arrival in New York
summary: The trip to New York took 16 days, two longer than expected because of adverse winds. Carl advises careful packing, good locks, and extra cash. He and his party arrived July 7, 1847, and stayed at the Greenwich House, 85 Greenwich Street.

title: IV. Inland to Milwaukee
summary: Carl and his party took the Newton, a Hudson River steamer to Albany, the train to Buffalo, and a Great Lakes steamship to Milwaukee — a far more comfortable part of the trip. He warns against taking the heavily marketed canal boats from Albany to Buffalo. Transportation inland is expensive, but the train is worth it.

title: V. First view of Calumet
summary: With baggage and belongings stashed in Milwaukee, Carl, Richard, and Eduard traveled by stagecoach to Fond du Lac, arriving July 27 in the evening. They went on foot to the Calumet settlement, where they stayed with Johann Mentis. Carl describes the topography in detail, with advice on how to find suitable land. After an exhausting expedition to see more of the territory, he bought a 40-acre farm next to Mentis.

title: VI. Citizenship and home
summary: Setting up a frontier household is expensive and difficult; clearing unbroken land is crushingly physical work. Carl describes the necessary equipment and lists prices. American axes are expensive but better than German ones. A featherbed is absolutely necessary; a clock, not so much.

title: VII. Life in America: Weather and Land
summary: Here, late in the pamphlet, Carl explains American weather, including tornadoes and wider-ranging temperatures than emigrants would leave behind in Germany, and explores the details of owning, clearing, and farming the land. It is back-breaking work.

title: VIII. Life in America: Crops, Livestock and People
summary: Carl offers information and advice on crops, livestock, game and wildfowl, and firearms. There are Indians on this frontier, some speaking good English and living in a settlement called Brothertown, others nomadic and living off the hunt.

title: IX. Final hints and Postscript
summary: Despite all the hardships and risks outlined in his pamphlet, Carl de Haas encouraged Germans who are considering emigration to make the move. He himself, however, as his brother Friedrich notes in the Postscript, left the frontier settler’s life after a year or so, set up a brewery with his brother and nephew, and then decamped for Buffalo, where he raised his family and worked as a journalist.

title: Chicago 1967, Part 1
author: Joel Nickel
summary: The call to Our Redeemer, and his predecessor’s advice: "Don’t come!" A parsonage with eighteen-inch walls and bars on the windows, and a church nobody had ever photographed from the neighbourhood’s side.

title: Chicago 1967, Part 2
author: Joel Nickel
summary: Hilmar Sieving, the congregation president who stayed in Woodlawn when the white families left and became a father to a pastor who had just lost his own. Vespers for a congregation of two, and the bald spot that announced the strain.

title: Chicago 1967, Part 3
author: Joel Nickel
summary: Seventeen hundred seats, an elderly white congregation and a young black one who had worshipped together for years without meeting. The silver communion cups donated when the first black member joined — and a crib death at Christmas.

title: Chicago 1968, Part 1
author: Joel Nickel
summary: Adult confirmations that showed how far the congregation had opened, urban renewal explained by the local bank, and a visit to a white parish that made the ride home to Englewood feel like coming back to safety.

title: Chicago 1968, Part 2
author: Joel Nickel
summary: The coal furnace, stoked by the pastor in full vestments ten minutes before the service. Dialogue sermons with a layman — the first at Our Redeemer — while members were still willing to drive in after dark.

title: Chicago 1968, Part 3
author: Joel Nickel
summary: Six hundred Parker High School students walked out over a school with no working sewing machines or gas jets, and came to the church because it was where they already met. Then King was murdered, and Malcolm X replaced him in the neighbourhood’s mind.

title: Chicago 1968, Part 4
author: Joel Nickel
summary: Where do two white people in a black ghetto fit? Refusing paternalism on one side and guilt on the other, and paying his dues to earn the name "blue-eyed soul brother."

title: Chicago 1968, Part 5
author: Joel Nickel
summary: Moving vans every week, landlords letting buildings rot toward an insurance claim, and a son stitched up in an emergency room with a bad reputation.

title: Chicago 1968, Part 6
author: Joel Nickel
summary: Otis Flynn arrives and the weekday congregation finds its advocate. A summer programme in the parking-lot playground, Joy Kristin born in July, and the first stirrings of the Englewood Welfare Rights Organization.

title: Chicago 1969, Part 1
author: Joel Nickel
summary: A seminar on the theology of hope, for a congregation short of it. Sue’s accident, and a janitor who would not accept help with a budget because he could not read.

title: Chicago 1969, Part 2
author: Joel Nickel
summary: A visiting college choir sang spirituals and the congregation’s intolerance "cut both ways" — then white members began selling tickets to a free pot-luck supper, and all hell broke loose. In church.

title: Chicago 1969, Part 3
author: Joel Nickel
summary: The Disciples asked to use the parish hall to stop the recruitment shootings, on three conditions: no guns, no drugs, no disrespect. Afterwards the building inspectors began calling.

title: Chicago 1969, Part 4
author: Joel Nickel
summary: Welfare Rights picketed the public aid office for a mother of eleven and won, and confidence in the organization grew. Operation Breadbasket put the local aldermen on notice from Our Redeemer’s own hall.

title: Chicago 1970, Part 1
author: Joel Nickel
summary: Visiting white church groups slept on the parsonage attic floor — an investment in understanding that still looked, to the neighbours, like a sightseeing tour. "Nice speech," said a visitor at the door.

title: Chicago 1970, Part 2
author: Joel Nickel
summary: The first Earth Day service, celebrated in work clothes: Eucharist, then brooms and shovels across three vacant lots. Two trees planted, and the last of the barbed wire taken off the fence.

title: Chicago 1970, Part 3
author: Joel Nickel
summary: Wyoming in August, far from the pressure-cooker — and a return to arson that was now deliberate rather than careless. The best Christmas tree they ever had, bought almost too late.

title: Chicago 1971, Part 1
author: Joel Nickel
summary: Attendance down to thirty-eight one January Sunday, counting pregnant women twice. A night in an airport terminal that taught him he was not constituted to be a community organizer.

title: Chicago 1971, Part 2
author: Joel Nickel
summary: The seventieth anniversary, celebrated in a big way partly because nobody expected a seventy-fifth: sixty-three in the morning, two hundred and fifty-five in the afternoon, and a sermon on the paradoxes of power.

title: Chicago 1971, Part 3
author: Joel Nickel
summary: The Redeemer Royals took second place, and former antagonists became the best confirmation class he ever taught. Tolerance under pressure, and the congregation’s own black dropouts.

title: Chicago 1972
author: Joel Nickel
summary: Seminars on youth in Englewood, a painting style of his own emerging at the Chicago Academy, and a riot downtown that prompted friends to write: "Wherever you go, you start riots."

title: Our Redeemer Lutheran Church, 1967-1972
summary: — Joel Nickel, Stayton, Oregon, Christmas 2011

series_title: Theodora and Ludwig / Muellers and Kniefs
title: Constanze Rösing: Aunt, friend, matchmaker
summary: Constanze Rösing’s niece Theodora Mueller emigrated with her parents and siblings to Kendallville, Indiana, in the fall of 1865 when she was 21. Ludwig Knief had already returned to Germany from the California gold fields by then. He was 23 and seeking theological training for his life’s goal: to serve as a Lutheran missionary in America. In 1863 he moved to Hermannsburg, where his circle of friends included Constanze, then 41. Constanze thought Ludwig and Theodora would make a great couple, and worked to bring them together. They were married in Kendallville in 1868.

title: My Ride: A 1976 Datsun 280Z
summary: In June 2022, Doug McMillan wrote and submitted this bit of autobiography to the *Wall Street Journal* for its “My Ride” feature.

title: Foot, Foot Foot, and Foot Foot Foot
summary: Ernie Mueller was, among other things, a born storyteller. No one knows whether “Foot, Foot Foot, and Foot Foot Foot” was his original composition, but his telling was highly original and memorable for a generation of nephews and nieces. In 1986, Ernie told it again to an assemblage of Muellers, asking the children to count the “foots.” His grand-niece Adele won the the grand prize, a moving wooden duck ornament for the garden. Ernie told and wrote the story several times. This version was in his own hand on three sheets (six sides) of ruled notebook paper, a keepsake of Ernie’s sister Adelheid.

title: Foot, Foot Foot, and Foot Foot Foot (a second telling)
summary: Ernie Mueller was, among other things, a born storyteller. No one knows whether “Foot, Foot Foot, and Foot Foot Foot” was his original composition, but his telling was highly original and memorable for a generation of nephews and nieces. Nephew Tim Mueller once asked him to write it down, and Ernie obliged — on both sides of a large sheet of paper. Tim transcribed it.

title: Obituary: Erhardt H. Essig
summary: Hardy Essig was easily the best professor of English literature in the Archivist’s long academic career. The classes he offered at Concordia Senior College in Fort Wayne — and the Archivist took all of them except the course on Milton, for scheduling reasons — were intellectually challenging and naturally engaging. The study of literature was never the same in graduate school. Hardy’s obituary ran in the Fort Wayne Journal-Gazette on April 5, 2006.

series_title: History and Rules of the Game
title: The Game of Five Rocks
summary: Some beachcombers make little piles of stones, call them cairns, and walk on. For the LeRoi-Nickel household in Portland, Oregon, that spur-of-the-moment creative task has evolved into a planful, aspirational, competitive art form evocative of work by the sculptor [Isamu Noguchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isamu_Noguchi) (1904–1988). The annual roster of invited participants grows; the rules continue to evolve.

title: *Biskuit oder Schwammkuchen*
summary:
**Sponge Cake (a.k.a., *Eierschwer*)**  
Mueller weddings and other ceremonial gatherings were never complete without a dense yellow sponge cake, often served with berries or other fruit. The Muellers called it *“Eierschwer”* (egg-heavy) because the recipe listed its ingredients based on the exact weight of the eggs. There were variations (eight eggs rather than 10), but the ingredients were always the same, always in exact proportion, and came with the strict instruction: Stir it in the same direction. This is the original from Frau Erica’s *Deutsch-Amerikanisches Kochbuch*.

title: Sauerbraten
summary: There are countless variations on the sauerbraten theme, from celery to stewed raisins, and many German families have their own recipes. This is from Frau Erica’s *Deutsch-Amerikanisches Kochbuch* (Rundschau Publishing Co., Milwaukee and Chicago, 1903; Eleventh printing).

title: A brother-in-law’s account of Paul Mueller’s wedding
summary: Fred Knief (above, with Dodo) read a congratulatory message from his brother-in-law Ernst (Opa) Mueller at the wedding celebration, then sent Ernst a full report, dated June 6, 1909. Only the [first page](https://www.frauerica.org/Images/_Image.php?refer=/Text/FredKnief1.php&image=0122) of Fred’s report survives:

title: Fritz Mueller’s Journal of The Voyage to America
author: Mark Nickel
summary:
For decades, the archive had only an English translation of Fritz Mueller’s journal, prepared by Fritz’s great-grandson Herbert Mueller. In September 2025, the archive received a 35-year-old photocopy of the original German Herbert used, found among papers in the estate of his son Robert. In October 2025, a web search found the original Mueller family copy, printed in Germany in 1867, in the collection of the Lilly Library at Indiana University-Bloomington. The library provided a high-resolution copy of the 18-page journal now
[available on FrauErica.org.](/galleries/32)

title: In Bremerhaven
author: Fritz Mueller
summary:
The Mueller family had begun its journey, although they were still at anchor offshore at Bremerhaven. Fritz began writing his journal by recounting bon voyage visits and farewell gifts presented before the steam tug pushed *der Adler* away from land. Gifts included butter, cookies, and apples.
[View the 1867 printed edition](/galleries/32)

title: On the High Seas
author: Fritz Mueller
summary: Dated entries from August 23 to September 2, as *der Adler* rounded Scotland between the Orkney and Shetland Islands. Fritz recounts dolphins under the surface, two exhausted falcons that landed on the rafts, and an argument with a New Yorker over who was to blame for the ship's slow progress. Then the storm struck off Fair Island, the last of Europe they would see. Theodora buried her head in her brother's chest; Friedrich asked his father whether they would all now go to the beautiful heaven. Fritz answered with Psalm 107, and with a poem of his own on the waves of the sea.

title: Shipboard Portraits
author: Fritz Mueller
summary: Fourteen days of rocking had thrown Fritz off his daily entries, so he set the diary aside for what he called an unbound narrative. Remedies for seasickness, and a warning about the first cabin's hinged doors, one of which crushed his thumb. Then the people: a brewer and a boy put in irons after a fight, whose temple Fritz stitched and dressed; a blacksmith from Constance who deserted the Baden army and slipped past the Bremen police; a girl of seventeen whom no one aboard would take in; and a Württemberg honeymoon couple whose husband he treated for bleeding.

title: Hunger and Hostilities
author: Fritz Mueller
summary: The hardest chapter of the journal. A spring-tide wind tore through six sails and nearly washed the children off the deck, and between the squalls Fritz set down the one portrait of his family the book holds, child by child. Then the ship's food failed. He fed an East Frisian baker's starving infant arrowroot from the medicine chest until the captain barred him from the lower deck; the child died and was lowered into the sea at midnight. Days later a New Yorker threw him over the pump handle, leaving him eight days in his bunk and his family unwilling to let him go up alone.

title: Arrival in New York
author: Fritz Mueller
summary: The pilot came aboard on September 30, and land appeared the next morning — a sight Fritz could compare only to standing as a child at the door while the Christmas tree was lit. A merchant named Auger took the whole family in, eleven of them sleeping in one room on a single bed and three straw mattresses. At Castle Garden an officer asked his name, then his home village, and proved to be the cousin who carried them through the formalities. Fritz closes with what the Bremen houses charged to release his own money, and a warning to anyone following him: take cash or bonds, never a bill of exchange.

title: Journey’s End in Indiana
author: Fritz Mueller
summary: The family left New York by train on the evening of October 5 and spent two nights in the cars. They were stranded among English speakers at Niagara Falls until a German innkeeper was fetched for them, and saw the falls that afternoon. At Cleveland they stayed with Pastor Wyneken, and learned what had become of the ship they had nearly sailed on instead: twelve dead at sea, and more after landing. Fritz settled on 560 acres and a sawmill near Kendallville, moved his family onto it on November 15, and closed the little book at the new year.

title: Early death and an epic land swindle
author: Mark Nickel
summary: The Mueller family had been in its new home less than half a year when it suddenly faced disaster. Fritz Mueller, age 44, died on May 6, 1866, and the family soon learned that all the land they had bought was encumbered by an undisclosed lien. They lost almost everything.

title: Gerhard Wilhelm Mueller: Boo-Boo
author: Mark Nickel
summary: Gerhard was the most reclusive and enigmatic of Ernst and Helen’s children. He served ever-smaller Lutheran parishes in Nebraska and northern Minnesota, subsisted below the poverty line for much of his adult life, and seemed only at home when he arrived — most often unannounced — to visit siblings. His siblings called him Gene (derived from a high school principal’s misunderstanding of “G. Mueller”) or *Päsel;* to neices and nephews, he was always Boo-Boo. No one really knew why.

title: Immer eine Freude in Height of Land zu predigen
author: Gerhard Mueller
summary:
Gerhard Mueller’s last Christmas letter to the California aunts, written December 20, 1969, and transcribed by his sister Frieda. Gerhard was serving St. John’s Lutheran Church in Height of Land, a congregation established by his uncle, the aunts’ brother Rev. Paul Gerhard Mueller.

With his unheated parsonage and unheated churches too cold for winter survival, Gerhard would move into the Morningside Motel in the fall and stay until the weather warmed reliably in the spring. He referred to the Morningside Motel as his “winter quarters.” No one seemed to know details about the annual arrangement — only that Gerhard was reasonably warm and safe during the worst part of the northern Minnesota winter.

The first sentence of Gerhard’s letter was written in German script. Gerhard sprinkled German script throughout his letters — more often than any of his siblings and sometimes to people he knew would not be able to decipher it.

title: Pastor’s Booming Cheers Invoke Tournament Win
author: Jim Klobuchar
summary: A Minneapolis Tribune reporter caught the Rev. Gerhard Mueller at Williams Arena, loosening his tie and bellowing “Atta boy, bay-bee, way to hustle” through Bemidji's 71-53 consolation win at the state tournament. A stout, ruddy-cheeked man of 57 with a voice from the drill field, he had followed the Bemidji team from border to border — and had given up Saturday night games because the congregation could not hear him from the pulpit the next morning.

title: Estate of Gerhard Mueller
author: Mark Nickel
summary:
I Timothy 6:7  
*“For we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out.”*  
Gerhard‘s total estate came to $1,124, nearly all of it junk.

title: A Road Trip Through Gerhard Country
author: Mark Nickel
summary: In December of 1980, the archivist had time and opportunity to drive through northern Minnesota — Tenstrike, Lake George, Frazee, Height of Land, Park Rapids, Bemidji — interviewing people who knew Gerhard and picking up bits and pieces of the historical record. Handwritten notes from that trip surfaced nearly 40 years later and are transcribed here.

title: Gerhard Wilhelm Mueller: 1904 – 1970
author: Becker County Record
summary: Although he had been a hardy person for most of his life, Gerhard’s health began to fail in the late 1960’s. Obesity, swelling in the extremities and possibly congestive heart disease or undiagnosed pre-diabetes led him occasionally to the *Wunderdoktoren* in Fargo. The obituary ran in the *Becker County Record* on Thursday, September 10, 1970, page 5. (See note below.)

summary: For years, H.C. Nickel taught evening business classes once or twice a week at Indiana University’s Gary campus. This description of H.C.’s introductory session for a family finances class ran the following April 30. Adelheid Nickel sent the author a dozen roses.

title: How *Der Struwwelpeter* came to be
summary: Beginning as a Christmas present in 1844, *Struwwelpeter* became one of the most successful children’s books ever. It went through hundreds of editions, was translated into all European and several other languages, and was a familiar part of life in the immigrant German home. This account, written by the author Heinrich Hoffmann, appeared in 1867, marking the 100th edition of the book.

title: A minister sues his congregation
summary: The $45,000 defamation suit — about $1.2 million in 2015 dollars — brought by the Rev. Charles L. Janzow, pastor of Bethlehem Evangelical Lutheran Church, against 18 members of his congregation in 1904, was withdrawn by mutual consent. Erich E.A. Mueller and his “Christian socialist” writings were a factor in the suit. The Synodical Proceedings of 1907 mention the controversy. Janzow himself was removed from the Missouri Synod but apparently was later restored. This is Janzow’s obituary from the *St. Louis Post-Dispatch*.

series_title: *Die Angelegenheit der Bethlehemsgemeinde zu St. Louis, Mo.*
title: (The Matter of the Bethlehem Congregation at St. Louis, Mo.)

The original German of the following account comes from the *1907 Proceedings of the Western District*, courtesy of the Concordia Historical Institute.

title: Brentwood Missouri
summary:
**II. Brentwood, Missouri**  
Jim’s studio in Brentwood, Missouri, was next door to Standard Pipe Protection Co., a business that wrapped sections of pipe in protective coatings for construction oil pipelines. It was a great place to scrounge for materials. The plywood end caps, which the company discarded when shipments of new pipe sections arrived, became raw material for his “Circle Pieces.”

title: New York, New York
summary:
**III. New York, New York**  
In 1978, Nickel loaded his work, supplies and equipment into a rental truck and left the St. Louis area for New York, where he opened a studio on the 11th floor of a building on 35th Street, a block from Macy’s. He later bought a building on Bedford Avenue in Brooklyn and moved his studio into what had once been a delicatessen.

title: An Arrest Reported in Powers, Michigan
summary: New Year’s Day 1924 found Joe King’s brother Lawrence jailed in Powers, Michigan. Police raided the pool room Lawrence operated in Powers, armed with a federal warrant charging him with illegal possession and sale of moonshine whiskey. Lawrence attempted to escape, running out the back door with a few bottles of “white mule” — a common term for moonshine because of its lack of color and its powerful kick, according to Merriam-Webster.

He continues to show his work in Oregon galleries and has had shows at the Keizer Community Center since 2018. He wrote the following essay for “Connective Relations,” his 2026 show at Keizer.

summary: Kevin was a ranger with the National Park Service for nearly 25 years. The following comes from the online NPS history entry for the Hubbell Trading Post, where Kevin once served as superintendent.

title: I. Introduction
summary: Ludwig Knief‘s *Lebenslauf* was circulated widely in the Mueller and Knief families. This copy arrived from Frieda Gilvarg, Fred and Dodo Knief‘s neice. It is dated August 1902, neatly typed, and accompanied by a typed *Nachtrag* (Epilogue), probably the work of Fred Knief in Milwaukee. The following translation is complete but still a work in progress. Some of the idiomatic 19th-century German was difficult to translate. Corrections and suggestions are always welcome.

title: II. Childhood
summary:
***Lebenslauf II:* Childhood and Confirmation**  
“My confirmation made a great impression on me. I cried and secretly made a selfish vow to God that if he would grant my wish and allow me to get out into the wider world, then I would speak the word of God to the Indians so that they could become Christians.”

title: III. Gold Rush
summary:
***Lebenslauf III:* First Emigration – The California Gold Rush**  
“When I emigrated at age 20, it had to happen secretly since I could not undertake a journey because of my approaching military obligation. But I had no scruples about avoiding that. In California I lived completely without God’s word and prayer, but even while I was in Bremen and went to the cathedral, I heard only rationalistic nonsense.”

title: IV. Back to Germany
summary:
***Lebenslauf IV:* The Return to Germany**  
“In Hermannsburg I made the acquaintance of one of the Fritschel brothers from the Iowa Synod. There were four of us there at the time who were studying for America, and he tried to persuade us to join the Iowa Synod. I refused to make that pledge on the grounds that I did not know enough about the doctrinal differences between the Missouri and Iowa synods to tell them apart.”

title: V. Mission in America
summary:
***Lebenslauf V:* Marriage and Mission in America**  
“I asked for the hand of a virtuous and marriageable young woman, Theodora Mueller, through her mother, the widow Johanna Mueller of Kendallville, Noble County, Indiana. We had never seen each other. I did not know her; she did not know me. I took this step on the advice of Theodora’s aunt, Miss Constance Rösing, whom I had met in Hermannsburg, and with trust in the gracious providence of God. ... We became engaged on the 17th and celebrated our wedding on the 24th of May 1868.”

title: VI. The Muellers
summary:
***Lebenslauf VI:* Theodora and the Mueller In-Laws**  
“My mother-in-law had a very difficult struggle. She had to endure the full measure of her widow’s burden, which she bore and overcame with patience and hope of eternal life. Most of her earthly goods were plundered by merciless money-lenders and a domineering, tyrannical pastor under whom my sainted father-in-law had already suffered greatly and had been deeply hurt.”

title: VII. Epilogue
summary:
***Lebenslauf VII:* Final Years and Epilogue**  
“He appealed to a member of his earlier congregation at Golden, a man named Heinrich Buss who was living in Nebraska, to advance him money with which to build a small house in Rosebud, Missouri, near his first congregation in Drake. Here, it seemed, he would have peace and domesticity. But this house was not going to be his final place on earth either, because on August 11, 1911, it burned to the ground with everything that was in it.”

title: Persons who fail to protect themselves against the plague ... are murderers
summary: Martin Luther, never one to mince words, recognized an individual’s responsibility for community public health. Not taking precautions against the plague and thereby infecting others would make people “responsible before God” for their neighbor’s death.

title: Christmas 1995
author: Mark Nickel
summary: The first letter in the archive, from a house full of teenagers. Dan has passed his mother in height at thirteen, Susan is twelve and newly in braces, and Anson is a third-grader two years into the violin. Alli is church organist and choir director; Mark manages the News Bureau at Brown. Alli’s father died in June.

title: Christmas 1998
author: Mark Nickel
summary: Dan is six foot two and drives himself to St. George’s; Susan has remade herself as a goalie for the Lincoln Lynx’s first-ever season, averaging thirty-five saves a game. For Mark’s fiftieth birthday, Alli commissioned a setting of three e.e. cummings love poems, premiered by the Providence Singers at Trinity Church in Newport.

title: Christmas 1999
author: Mark Nickel
summary: Written in what the letter calls the Time of the Naked Lemons — the stripped lemons piling up in the fridge from a seventh loaf of *Stollen*. Dan is hunting for colleges, Susan is learning to drive from a crusty detachment of Providence police officers, and Alli has won a Rhode Island Foundation fellowship to study how community choruses turn professional.

title: Christmas 2000
author: Mark Nickel
summary: The year Anson was diagnosed with diabetes, in May, and absorbed it so matter-of-factly that his parents’ worry became the harder problem. Dan is a freshman at Vermont, Susan a senior weighing colleges, and Anson is bound for Tabor. Mark makes good on his threat to acquire agricultural machinery.

title: Christmas 2001
author: Mark Nickel
summary: Dan leaves for a semester in Seville, Susan transfers to the School of the Museum of Fine Arts, and Anson is the only freshman skating for Tabor’s JV-A. Alli becomes the Providence Singers’ first executive director, and both parents make their Symphony Hall debut singing what Mark defines as antler music with the Boston Pops.

title: Christmas 2002
author: Mark Nickel
summary: Six holiday concerts with the Boston Pops, and a gentler year otherwise. Dan is back from Seville and a junior at Vermont, Susan a sophomore in Boston, Anson invited to spring lacrosse training in Florida. Alli gets a home office in Anson’s old bedroom, and Mark discovers that a warming climate will ripen artichokes in New England.

title: Christmas 2003
author: Mark Nickel
summary: A year measured in telephone calls — Dan ringing up with questions about opera, Susan about Beethoven’s late quartets, and both of them about how long you can keep hamburger. Anson skips hockey for the first time since he was five in order to train for lacrosse. The garden takes on horseradish, garlic and heirloom tomatoes.

title: Christmas 2004
author: Mark Nickel
summary: Mark and Alli sang Dave Brubeck’s *The Gates of Justice* with Brubeck himself on opening night of the fiftieth Newport Jazz Festival; he called it the best performance in his thirty years with the piece. Anson is admitted to Brown early decision, Alli shoots a hole-in-one, and Mark begins editing Fritz Mueller’s 1865 journal — the first work of this archive.

title: Christmas 2005
author: Mark Nickel
summary: Anson’s first year at Brown, with four-in-the-morning emails from the computer science building and an internship at WBRU that turned into a paid job. The Providence Singers reach Lincoln Center with a Brubeck première. *The Muellers in America* reaches version 1.2, and Mark wonders whether to put the whole thing on a website.

title: Christmas 2006
author: Mark Nickel
summary: Eleven humpback whales breaching in unison off Alaska, and a sorrel harvest in December. Dan is living on the Paseo across from the Prado, Anson is a sophomore at Brown pulling the third-shift DJ slot at WBRU, and Susan is studying interior design at Suffolk. Mark passes twenty-five years at Brown.

title: Christmas 2007
author: Mark Nickel
summary: The letter in which this archive is first named. Mark and his three brothers tour Mueller and Nickel sites in the Midwest for what would have been their parents’ hundredth birthday — Hib and Addie were born the same day — and he comes home with two shovelfuls of farm dirt for the garden and a plan for a family history website: frauerica.org.

title: Christmas 2008
author: Mark Nickel
summary: Every Christmas tree lot was closed and mulched by the time they went looking; they found one behind the manure at a garden centre. Dan starts law school in Minnesota, Susan graduate work in Washington, and Anson enters his last semester at Brown into a collapsing job market. The Singers release their first commercial recording, Lukas Foss’s *The Prairie*.

title: Christmas 2009
author: Mark Nickel
summary: Flu put Mark and Alli in the audience for *Messiah* — the first time they had ever heard the Providence Singers from the other side, and it was a reassuringly wonderful sound. Anson graduates from Brown and begins architecture at Columbia, Dan is in China on law school credit, and Susan is studying French in Annecy.

title: Christmas 2010
author: Mark Nickel
summary: They drove up I-95 from Washington into the Boxing Day Blizzard of 2010 and rode it out on what was in the house: two kinds of herring, pancake mix, apples and *Springerle*. Anson has started at New York Legal Assistance Group, Susan is adding teacher certification, and Dan has just finished his final law school exam. The Year of the Cardoon is judged a failure.

title: Christmas 2011
author: Mark Nickel
summary: The cardoons nobody wanted to eat came back on their own and turned out to be the most beautiful thing on the property. Dan finishes law school and decamps for Madrid to start a business; Susan becomes a certified art teacher; Anson and Reva are in Manhattan applying to graduate schools. In Florence, thoroughly lost, Mark and Alli blunder into the *David*.

title: Christmas 2012
author: Mark Nickel
summary: Written as a market report. The *Stollen* count is down to two, *Springerle* and *Lebkuchen* futures are at all-time lows, and the bottom has fallen out of eggnog — but the fundamentals are sound. A travertine terrace goes in, niece Elsa plays beach volleyball for Spain at the Olympics, and after twenty-six years of marriage the two of them birdie the seventeenth simultaneously.

title: Christmas 2013
author: Mark Nickel
summary: Susan and George marry in Washington inside a two-hour window of blue sky in a day of steady rain, and in October comes word from Brooklyn that Anson and Reva are engaged. Mark turns a crop of cabbage into sauerkraut by Frau Erica’s method, in a stone crock, from a plot carrying a shovelful of dirt from the Kendallville farm.

title: Christmas 2014
author: Mark Nickel
summary: Alli retires after sixteen years running the Providence Singers and becomes Executive Director Emerita. Mark works out that he has been at Brown for 13.6 percent of its entire history and has served under 28.9 percent of its presidents. Three dwarf cherry trees, condemned and facing the power saw, are saved by radical pruning.

title: Christmas 2015
author: Mark Nickel
summary: The year the circle closed. A hundred and fifty years after Fritz Mueller sold *Bosenbüttel* and boarded ship at Bremerhaven, Mark and Alli punched the name into a rented Nissan’s GPS and found themselves in the farmyard an hour later, talking with Rainer Stoll, who listened and then asked: *“Heißt er Fritz?”* Anson and Reva married in Brooklyn in June.

title: Christmas 2016
author: Mark Nickel
summary: Thomas Crawley Knowles is born in Washington on July 30, the same day his great-grandmother turned ninety-seven, and Mark and Alli officially style themselves Opa and Oma. Dan’s Tierra is up to five restaurants in Madrid, and Mark redesigns the Frau Erica Project, then chronicling 1,021 Muellers in America.

title: Christmas 2018
author: Mark Nickel
summary: Two grandsons in one year: Archer Gaur Nickel in Brooklyn on May 2, and James Mark Knowles in Richmond on September 22. The Galapagos in late summer — snorkelling with sea turtles, a volcano lighting up the night sky, Darwin’s own trails. Six new fruit trees go in, planted against a future batch of *Pflaumenmus*.

title: Christmas 2019
author: Mark Nickel
summary: The old sports closet, once a hazard of hockey helmets and lacrosse pads, now holds Yak Trax from a winter trip to Yellowstone, and the garden gets raised beds and stepping-stone paths — accommodations as much as improvements. Alli begins coping with the symptoms she calls the wobblies. The squirrel-proof Corn Palace finally brings in a popcorn harvest.

title: Christmas 2020
author: Mark Nickel
summary: Leia Reva Nickel arrives in Brooklyn on December 10, the brightest thing in what the letter calls an *annus horribilis*. Covid ends choral singing — the Singers’ fiftieth season dissolves into Zoom rehearsals and virtual-choir recordings. The tree is chest-high this year, and the letter closes on e.e. cummings.

title: Christmas 2021
author: Mark Nickel
summary: Dan and Aliki marry in the mountain village of Agios Lavrentios, in the country the Centaurs come from. At home, Alli is recovering from a fall and from the illness now named: MSA. The Providence Singers commission a Julian Wachner setting of Sara Teasdale dedicated to the two of them. Its title is *We Two Alone*.

title: Christmas 2022
author: Mark Nickel
summary: Olivia Eirene Crawley Kantikou is born in Madrid on December 7, five days after her cousin Adriana and three days before Leia’s second birthday. Ramps now make the whole first floor reachable, and the Studebaker — an all-terrain wheelchair, a gift from Alli’s siblings — takes them back onto the trails at Sachuest and the Norman Bird Sanctuary.

title: Christmas 2023
author: Mark Nickel
summary: Thomas and James, six and four, sat cross-legged at the end of the driveway in their pyjamas waiting for the garbage truck, and the driver climbed down and gave them the whole show. The *Sängerbote* arrives from brother Timothy — seven hundred pages of a St. Louis German quarterly with Frau Erica among its contributors. Black knot takes the three cherry trees.

title: Christmas 2024
author: Mark Nickel
summary: No travel this year, but a Hoyer lift they have christened the Flying Oma Device lifts Alli out of bed each morning and into the day. Granddaughter Leia pulls a copy of *Struwwelpeter* out from under the coffee table and launches a project, and the *Sängerbote* compendium — all fifty-five Mueller contributions — is finished.

title: Christmas 2025
author: Mark Nickel
summary: The mystery of Fritz’s German original is solved. A photocopy forwarded by Theresa Delaplain sent Mark hunting, and the Lilly Library at Indiana turned out to hold not a copy but *the* 1867 Mueller family heirloom, an exact smudge-for-smudge match. Alli still contends valiantly with MSA, though speaking is now very difficult.

title: Obituary: Martin E. Mueller
summary: This obituary ran in the *Green Bay Press-Gazette*, Green Bay, WI, on January 15, 2003

title: Allison McKibbin’s engagement ring
summary: The diamond solitaire has been in the family for four generations — originally as an engagement ring, then as a solitaire necklace — and has resided in Minnesota, Europe, Rhode Island, and currently in Richmond, Virginia.

title: Otto Mueller on the original Mueller farm
summary: Otto was about 8 years old when when his parents sold their small farm at Story Lake, near Kendallville, and acquired the original Mueller farm. Otto grew up to become a Lutheran minister. He is buried in the churchyard of St. John’s in Kendallville. This comes from an extensive memoir Otto wrote in retirement.

title:
My Life and Its Times  

Mary Allison (Molly) Bigelow McMillan
summary: Molly McMillan — Nana, to her grandchildren and great-grandchildren — had a lot to distill into a memoir: daughter of a long-established Twin Cities family, physics graduate of Vassar, war-time bride, early feminist, civic leader, among the first ordained Presbyterian women in Minnesota, mother of five, grandmother of 15, great-grandmother of 10. She worked on the following chapters for several years, signing and dating the memoir on All Saints Day, November 1, 2007. Life — and great-grandchildren — kept coming for nearly another decade.

title: Foreword
summary: Molly”s forebears — Bigelows, McKibbins, Dorseys, Dorrises — were English or Scots-Irish. They arrived in St. Paul from New York, Massachusetts, and Pennsylvania in the mid-19th century — and they thrived.

title: Back Home
summary: Molly’s experience as a regional officer for the Junior League prepared her for positions of community leadership in St. Paul and Ramsey County as well as for service on various foundation boards.

title: Road to Ministry
summary: Molly had returned to the House of Hope after college. Her experience there deepened, including election as an elder and a seminal study group of churchwomen. Studies at United Theological Seminary, originally as part of a graduate program, deepened as well.

series_title: My Way Comes Through Thee, O God
title: My Way Through Thee
summary: In her section on “The Unlikely Road to Ministry,” Molly describes a night of contemplation and spiritual awakening. When she took up her pen the next morning, she felt an almost automatic jotting of the phrase, “My way comes through thee, O God.” This is the poem she created then.

series_title: United Theological Seminary of the Twin Cities
title: The Seminary
summary: Ordained and well-experienced in leading a large congregation, Molly returned to United Theological Seminary as interim president, then chair of the Board, and finally as fundraiser and patron for Bigelow Chapel.

title: Trees
summary: Trees were important to Molly, both as trees and as metaphors for grouping and fixing memories. When she wrote about her father, she wrote also about [the woods](/documents/192). She wrote “Trees” at another turning point in her life, when she left Manitou Island and moved to her apartment at EagleCrest.

title: The Years Alone
summary: Five years after her husband died, Molly sold the home on Manitou Island and moved to an apartment in EagleCrest, a Presbyterian Home in Roseville, Minnesota. She traveled, continued to do “supply preaching” in congregations with vacancies, and found ways to further pursue some of the intellectual and theological questions that intrigued her.

title: Poetic Odds and Ends
summary: Molly‘s computer had a lot of writing on it — sermons, poetry, beginnings of documents, sketches of times and places. Some of these she expanded and incorporated into her memoir. “Poetic Odds and Ends” was the final part of her memoir, a mosaic of verses she evidently found pleasing or important but couldn’t find a place for.

title: My Father
summary: C.H. Bigelow Jr., Molly’s father, was a widower with three children when he married Molly’s mother, Allison McKibbin. C.H. was 53 when Molly was born; newborn Molly had three young-adult siblings aged 18, 21, and 24.

title: The Woods
summary: Molly was a perceptive and versatile writer. Her memoir includes several original poems and a collection of poetic odds and ends. “The Woods” celebrates her father’s “other great love.”

title: My Mother
summary: Although she did not feel close to her mother, Molly did learn learn some important things from her: how to write, that injustice must be confronted forcefully ... and how to knit.

title: Childhood
summary: Summers found Molly on Manitou Island, a Bigelow retreat that was “a summer playground for for its many children in the 1920s and ’30s.” Her children and grandchildren knew exactly what she meant.

title: Education
summary: Molly was a pioneer, the only physics major in the Vassar Class of 1941. She understood the physics of what she could not see — atoms, waves, particles — but the mathematics that described observable physical forces, not so much. Music, however, was a lifelong joy.

title: Marriage and Children
summary: Dick and Molly were two very different people, Molly wrote, but they shared a great range of interests, including a healthy dose of international golfing.

title: The Hummingbird
summary: An observation triggers memory of a vignette from decades ago.

title: The Junior League
summary: As a new college graduate, Molly was invited to join the Junior League. She thrived on the opportunity, developing her administrative skills and rising to become a regional director.

title: Obituary: The Rev. E.H.C. Mueller (Der Lutheraner)
summary: The following *Todesanzeige*, written *auf Deutsch* by the Rev. Herbert C. Mueller, Opa’s son, appeared on page 356 of *Der Lutheraner*, “The Official Organ of The Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod,” on October 26, 1948. An obituary *auf Englisch* also appeared in [*The Lutheran Witness*](/documents/201) for October 5, 1948, on page 324.

title: Obituary: Peter Albert Crawley
summary: Peter’s parents lived in Hamden, Connecticut, about five miles north of New Haven. He was returning to Rhode Island after visiting his father, who had been hospitalized in New Haven.

title: Obituary: Richard William Gahl
summary: Dick Gahl and Joel Nickel, classmates at Concordia Seminary in St. Louis, shared a Mueller heritage. Dick’s grandmother Emma, daughter of Enno Mueller, and Joel’s grandfather Ernst, son of Wilhelm Mueller, were cousins.

title:
Obituary  
Robert Kent Mueller
summary: Robert Kent Mueller, the fifth child of Herbert and Ruth (Polley) Mueller, was a composer, orchestral conductor, organist and veteran music professor at the University of Arkansas.

title: History of St. John’s Thrift Shop
summary: This history, written by Laura Mellenthin in May 1977, was sent by Mary Jo Uebele in response to a request from the archivist for historic information about the St. John’s Thrift Shop, founded by Adelheid Schumm and other members. It opened on June 29, 1970, and is still operating.

title: Shirley Jean King (1947–2022)
summary: (optional)

title: Stollen, a Christmas Bread
summary: A lighter, tastier, more wholesome German Christmas bread without a hint of candied fruit. Stollen baking is to be done only between Thanksgiving and the following January 6, the Feast of the Epiphany. It is legal to bake a final loaf on the sixth, slice it, wrap it carefully in portions, and freeze it for enjoyment later in the year.

title: Tante Fieks: Bright and Dark Days (Part 2)
summary: Here follows a biographical essay by Frieda Katharine Magdalena Caroline Mueller Feiertag (a.k.a., Tante Fieks). Fieks apparently wrote this at age 84 for — perhaps at the invitation of — her nieces Frieda Elizabeth Mueller and Adelheid Mueller Nickel.

title: Johanne’s money belt, Georg’s tobacco box
summary:
The wooden box, a cube about six inches on a side, may have been in the family before Georg received it. It was handed down from Georg to Fritz to Wilhelm to Ernst (Opa) to son Ernst (Uncle Ernie of Eagle Lake), and eventually to Ernie’s nephew Herbert. It was accompanied by a
[handwritten note](https://www.frauerica.org/Images/_Image.php?refer=$refer&image=0564)
from Opa Mueller, transcribed below.

title: Anna’s history, Part II
summary:
**Part Two: Marriage, family, West Ely, Missouri, and Woodworth, Illinois**  
Anna Wolter and Henry Waldschmidt — she first knew him as “Jake” — went their separate ways after high school. Henry went off to college; Anna took a job at the phone company. They met again as maid of honor and best man at the wedding of mutual friends.

title: II. Careers in Chicago
summary:
**II. Careers in Chicago**  
With their early years on the Mueller Farm behind them, Wilhelm and Adelheid began to look toward the next chapter. Wilhelm’s work as a drayman in Kendallville was a temporary measure. In less than two years they were off to Chicago, where Adelheid would continue her career as a writer under the pen name Frau Erica and Wilhelm would begin more than three decades of service as superintendent of Concordia Cemetery.

title: III. Muellers in America
summary:
**III. The Muellers are in America to stay**  
Wilhelm and Frau Erica lived into their 70s and celebrated their silver and golden wedding anniversaries with their children. (A copy of the engraved silver invitation is in the archives.)

title: Wilhelm Mueller: Cemetery Superintendent
summary:
***Forest Leaves*** for June 7, 1918  
One measure of Wilhelm Mueller’s stature in suburban Chicago was that his obituary was carried as the cover story in *Forest Leaves.* This comes from the files of his granddaughter Frieda Mueller Gilvarg.

title: SS Lessing Manifest, 1879
summary: Michael and Wilhelmine Nickel left Prussia for America in 1879, carrying an infant son and whatever fit in steerage. Their arrival on the SS Lessing — recorded name by name on the ship's own passenger manifest — is the oldest surviving record of this branch of the family in the United States.
